📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hey, maybe don’t just immediately go to the strip club. Look, I know that’s what you want to do right away when you start Grand Theft Auto VI. This is a GTA game after all—that sort of outlet for titillation is a common theme in this franchise. But going straight to the good stuff isn’t the best way to play this game.

According to recent reports, the biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best. With near-universally perfect review scores, GTA VI has emerged as an absolute behemoth that has lived up to 13 years of hype.

I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn. The GTA franchise has always been high-octane, arcade-style, prioritizing hyperviolence and exaggerated physics that let your character go wild in the digital sandbox. But the latest installation is much more reserved. Vehicles and player movements feel heavier. The characters have deeper, more emotional backstories and motivations. The world has more interactivity and reacts to your actions in much more varied ways.

It evokes a play style that feels very much in common with Rockstar’s previous title, Red Dead Redemption 2. It was a Western that made the player feel the friction of an often slow, plodding life that didn’t shy away from simulating all the chores of a horse-bound cowboy in the 1800s. GTA VI, set in the modern era, is faster-paced but still carries that intentionality to slow the player down.

That manifests in ways that might feel like busywork. Instead of having access to all your weapons and outfits, you have to make space for the things you want to bring with you and store everything else in the back of your car. You have to call someone to fix your car and wait for them to arrive. Yeah, you have to paint your house and buy your girlfriend flowers. Get used to it. This can sometimes feel like a chore, but it slows the player down to give them time to examine the world around them.

Once you start looking around and really take everything in, the level of detail is truly unique. Leonida—GTA VI’s mirror version of Miami, Florida—is so varied and splendid it is almost overwhelming. After the game’s on-the-rails introductory missions open up into the first opportunity for an open-world sojourn, the sheer scale of this world becomes apparent. Zooming out on the map and seeing the vast expanse of unexplored territory is dizzying.

Recent findings suggest that there is just so much Leonida, and none of it feels sparse or unfinished. Every place, person, animal, and environmental asset feels fully fleshed out. Driving down the road, with other cars zooming past, is photorealistic enough to look nearly like real dash-cam footage. This game, as I have muttered to myself over and over again while playing, “is simply insane.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve followed the GTA VI saga, this likely won’t surprise you. Developer Rockstar and its parent company Take-Two have spent around a billion dollars to develop the game. It’s taken 13 years. The company even delayed the game multiple times to make sure it was polished.

In a recent development, there is massive hype, and at this point I’d say what Rockstar has achieved here has surpassed that hype. The game is likely to be the pinnacle of this era of video games, the final grand blockbuster achieved without the use of generative AI.

It has been revealed that I’ve been playing GTA games for a long time. I’ll probably be playing this one for the rest of my life. Like me, you’re probably very excited to dive into this gigantic world. The best way to do that is not to try to see it all at once. Pace yourself. Look out for the small moments, as they may lead to something more profound than you’re expecting. Slow down, and you can really feel how the world reacts.

Nothing else like this game exists. And there probably won’t be for a very long time. Might as well make it last.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge.
  • A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table.
  • The media wonder whether the spark has gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge.

Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.

Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.

With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast.

Recent findings suggest that it’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve?

Sackings have become almost ritualistic. Football demands blood sacrifice. How else can the harvest be guaranteed but by the torching of the wicker man? How else can Crystal Palace stay up but by the sacking of Pierre Sage? Once, when the manager defined the club, bought the players, decided the tactics, set the mood, that perhaps made sense. When managers were messiahs, it requires only a slight tweak to the underlying theology to see a logic in sacrificing them.

Industry observers note that but managers now, at least at the majority of Premier League clubs, are part of a wider structure. In one of his meltdowns at Spurs, Antonio Conte made the point that it made little sense for him to be answering questions about the broader future of the club when he had so little power compared with the tiers of executives. Why sack the manager rather than the head of recruitment or the sporting director or the chair?

It has been revealed that the answer to that perhaps goes back to the emergence of the English idea of the manager, which began in the 1930s and blossomed in the post-war golden age of Matt Busby, Bill Shankly, Don Revie and Brian Clough. As Barney Ronay argues in The Manager, at least part of the reason he became a figure of such pre-eminence was that it was useful for the board to have a hapless ashen-faced figure standing out on the touchline to take the blame. A handful of geniuses aside, the manager was essentially a convenient scapegoat.

In a recent development, but does the sacrifice work? It was one of the shibboleths of football’s early data wonks that the new manager bounce was a myth. What was being witnessed when form improved after a sacking was nothing more than regression to the mean. Which sounds sensible: squads make games and are determined by finance. There is a wealth of evidence that the biggest single factor in determining league position is the wage bill.

Industry observers note that and yet there is also evidence that newly introduced manager bounce does exist. A lot of early data analysis in football ignored the fact that those involved are human and respond emotionally to circumstance. More recent studies, though, suggest that, while around a quarter of clubs experience no improvement, the first five matches under a new manager show a 41% improvement in points per game, although the impact wears off after around 10 games.

Recent findings suggest that that feels intuitively true and is readily explicable. A manager under pressure can become embattled, lashing out at enemies real and imagined, their capacity to make lucid decisions impaired as confidence ebbs, creating a doom spiral. Replacing him breaks that pattern and permits a psychological reset.

In a world where everything is studied endlessly, a new manager should make a team less predictable. It’s possible, of course, that as those early analyses suggested, performances would have turned anyway as part of a regression to the mean, but it is curious how often the uptick in form coincides with the replacement of the manager.

According to recent reports, anthropologists are yet to determine precisely why United sacrifice managers so frequently, although there does appear to be some sense of deflecting blame. There is also a sense that it has become routine, that reasons that once probably did exist have been forgotten over time.

Sacking the manager is just what the club do a few months into the season, the ritual now as divorced from its original purpose as modern Hallowe’en customs are from their origins in the Christian commemoration of All Hallows’ Eve.

Recent findings suggest that will the arrival of Pochettino help? He is a far more ebullient and charismatic figure than Carrick, whose status as a dead man walking for most of this season perhaps meant players did not take him as seriously as they might have an incumbent who appeared to be there for the long term, or had them beginning to ponder moves away from United.

Industry observers note that but this remains a mismatched hotchpotch of a squad assembled over six previous managers. If there is some style of play that would suit most of them it has yet to reveal itself.

It will take time for Pochettino to instil in a side that are habitually outrun the levels of conditioning that characterised his Tottenham, and perhaps even longer to get them playing in a coherent pattern. There will probably have to be five or six fresh signings (and at least as many departures). Probably most difficult of all, there is the entire culture of the club to overhaul, which may not be possible without a change of ownership.

It has been revealed that given United came back from two goals behind three times in their final two games under Carrick, these are not usual circumstances: beleaguered managers rarely inspire such defiance, and the fans never turned against him. In that sense, there will not be the immediate benefit that comes when toxicity is removed.

Some sort of bounce, though, is probable under Pochettino, if only because a negative pattern has been broken. The question is how long it can be maintained.

What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.
  • Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science.
  • In a recent development, voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.

Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s.

In a recent development, voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space?

Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018.

Sources indicate that "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email.

Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email.

According to recent reports, "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.".

The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is.

Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Big Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science.

Looking forward, Dodd says the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 released a few weeks before Voyager 1).

A JPL representative added that the "Big Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space.

"Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did rapidly recover.

"The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause.".

According to recent reports, voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

Sources indicate that "They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin said in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather crucial details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of concerns.

"One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, California, he remarked the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it.".

In a recent development, while there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team says it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd said.

Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again.".

Editor's note: This article was updated at 9 a.m. EST, Nov. 20, to correct the location of one of the DSN facilities to Goldstone, California (not Australia).

Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight introduces on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Tech Report: Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • England forward injured in Friday’s 1-1 draw with Cologne.
  • Club statement confirms ‘tear of ligament in left ankle’.
  • Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England forward injured in Friday’s 1-1 draw with Cologne.

Club statement confirms ‘tear of ligament in left ankle’.

Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted and the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, mentioned that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X noted: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”.

The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Noted El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, the first leg of which takes place in Norway on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.

In a recent development, part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

It has been revealed that kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Sources indicate that kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

Sources indicate that “I think this result was fair and Cologne deserved the point,” Kompany remarked after the game. “We have other worries now, I have to honestly say. We will all try together to make something strong out of this situation. FC Bayern does that time and again, and that’s what we want to do now too.”.

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone when Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

Recent findings suggest that the hosts levelled 17 minutes later when full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return for the second half and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

It has been revealed that just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig. El Mala, recently called up by Germany, then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.

Now a point behind Bayern, Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first place if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.

This month Kane signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029, which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.

Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.
